name: Nora Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nora, thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I write the copy and plan the campaigns for a family-owned furniture company. We make solid wood tables, beds and sofas and sell them through our own showrooms and catalogue. A normal day is writing product descriptions, checking photos for the catalogue and planning the spring and autumn sales. I love writing about the craft, like how long the oak dries; I get tired of the online advertising side, which feels like shouting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any of the new AI tools at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No, never. The owners' son tried to get us using one last year, and I just carried on as I was. I'm engaged to Mateo, who's an electrician, and we're getting married next summer. We rent a small place near my parents and I've got about three months of costs saved, plus the wedding fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I think that's quite likely, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I knew it, people get carried away with new gadgets. I wouldn't post anything; I'm not online much. At church I'd probably say something like that to my aunt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel safe. The family who own our furniture company still sign every catalogue themselves, and a bit of clever software isn't going to change how they do things. They value people who've been there and know the products.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. I'd keep saving for the wedding and keep a little extra aside. I might ask the owners if I could help in the showroom more, because I like talking to customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in your life that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The wedding costs, if I'm honest. Mateo's work is steady, but everything costs more than we planned. But that's normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the showroom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like seeing people run their hands over the tables. It makes the words I write feel real.

say: I'd say people get **carried away** with new gadgets.
I'd say so to my **aunt** at church rather than online.
think: I privately feel **safe** at a family-owned firm.
The owners value people who **know the products** and have stayed for years.
do: Carry on with my work **as normal**.
Keep saving for the **wedding** and a little extra.
Ask to help more in the **showroom**.
S0.quote: The family who own our furniture company still sign every catalogue themselves, and a bit of clever software isn't going to change how they do things.
fieldNote: She trusts the **owning family** to value loyal staff.
Her pressure is **wedding costs**, which she treats as normal life.
She is drawn to **customer contact** in the showroom.

steps.text: Keep writing furniture catalogue copy by hand
Keep adding to the wedding fund and a small reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing and planning and answering customers. That's my job, right there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, and that we're losing something about real craft. I'd tell people I'll keep doing things properly. I wouldn't make a fuss at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be worried. I'd be the only person in the office still writing sofa descriptions with a pen, and I know exactly how that looks to the people paying me. The owners' son would push the tools and his parents would eventually listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to move into the showroom full time, where I can sell and talk to people. I'd keep more savings and maybe trim the wedding a bit. I'd talk to Mateo about helping with his paperwork in the evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like the ground's moving and I'm standing still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the tools to keep your desk job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little, if they made me. But I'd rather sell furniture face to face than type into a machine all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you cut the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer guests, maybe. My mother would hate it. But I'd rather start married life without debt.

say: I'd say it's a **shame** to lose real craft.
I'd say I'll keep doing things **properly**, without a fuss.
think: I privately worry I'd look **outdated** writing with a pen.
The **owners' son** would push the tools and win eventually.
do: Ask to move into the **showroom** full time.
Keep more savings and **trim the wedding**.
Help with Mateo's **paperwork** in the evenings.
feel: I feel **anxious**, like the ground moves while I stand still.
S1.quote: I'd be the only person in the office still writing sofa descriptions with a pen, and I know exactly how that looks to the people paying me.
fieldNote: She expects the **owners' son** to win the argument for AI.
She'd choose **face-to-face selling** over learning the tools.
She'd **shrink the wedding** rather than start married life in debt.

steps.text: Ask the owners for a full-time showroom sales role
Cut the wedding guest list to stay out of debt
Do Mateo's invoices and quotes in the evenings for pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Oh, that's very soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've lost our minds rushing into this. I'd say families and churches will have to hold people together, because the government won't. I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd expect to lose my job. If my job goes in two years, I'd go and do the books and the adverts for my fiancé Mateo's electrical business, because family looks after family. His work is hands-on, so it should last a few years longer than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start helping Mateo properly straight away, doing his quotes, invoices and his small website. I'd keep the wedding on but make it smaller. I'd talk to my parents about living with them for a while if money got tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Mateo's work is safer for three years. And after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. Maybe robots can't wire an old house. Maybe they can. We'd just have to keep going and trust it works out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept government help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If there was nothing else, yes. But I'd try family first. That's how I was raised.

I'd say **families and churches** will have to hold people together.
think: I privately expect to **lose my job** within two years.
Mateo's **hands-on work** should last a few years longer than mine.
do: Start doing Mateo's **quotes and invoices** straight away.
Keep the wedding on but make it **smaller**.
Ask my parents about **living with them** if needed.
feel: I feel **alarmed**, with my stomach dropping.
S2.quote: If my job goes in two years, I'd go and do the books and the adverts for my fiancé Mateo's electrical business, because family looks after family.
fieldNote: She turns to **family work** first, not the state.
She sees the **robot gap** as protecting Mateo's trade for a while.
She'd accept **government help** only as a last resort.

steps.text: Take over quotes, invoices and website for Mateo's electrical business
Ask her parents about moving in if money gets tight
Hold a smaller wedding next summer as planned
Cut back to essentials while the wedding is paid

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a little better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast, but at least people can see it coming. I'd say families should start planning together now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still expect to lose my job, just later. Five years is enough to get married, help my fiancé Mateo build his electrical firm, and still have a little money put aside when the marketing job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get married as planned and start helping Mateo with his paperwork. I'd save hard, maybe four or five months. I'd stay at the furniture company as long as they'd have me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, but there's time to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go into Mateo's firm full time eventually?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. He's been talking about taking on an apprentice. I could run the office side and he could do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing about the oak and walnut. I'd miss the smell of the workshop when I go down to check the photos.

say: I'd say it's still **too fast**, but people can see it coming.
I'd say **families** should start planning together now.
think: I privately expect to **lose my job**, just later.
Five years is enough to **get married** and help Mateo's firm grow.
do: Save hard toward **four or five months** of costs.
Stay at the furniture company **as long as possible**.
feel: I feel still **alarmed**, but with time to breathe.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to get married, help my fiancé Mateo build his electrical firm, and still have a little money put aside when the marketing job goes.
fieldNote: She still expects **job loss** and plans to join Mateo's firm.
Five years lets her **keep the wedding** intact.
She'd miss the **craft** of writing about wood.

steps.text: Marry Mateo next summer as planned
Save toward four or five months of costs
Keep writing for the furniture company as long as they'll have her

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's more like it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives families and communities time to prepare. I'd say people should learn real skills, not just screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel less frightened. Ten years is time enough to learn a proper trade from my uncle, the way my grandmother always said every girl in our family should. My uncle Rafa is a joiner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep my job and get married. I'd save steadily. In a few years I'd start learning joinery or furniture finishing with my uncle on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Joinery is hands-on. Robots come in 2039 in this picture. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But by 2039 I'd be 40, with my own skills, maybe children. I'd rather be good at something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want children in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in two or three years. Mateo and I both want a family. Ten years makes that feel possible.

say: I'd say a **decade** gives families and communities time to prepare.
I'd say people should learn **real skills**, not just screens.
think: I privately feel **less frightened** with ten years.
I'd learn a **proper trade** from my uncle, as my grandmother advised.
do: Start learning **joinery** with my uncle on weekends.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but with a direction.
S4.quote: Ten years is time enough to learn a proper trade from my uncle, the way my grandmother always said every girl in our family should.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her plan a **trade** through family ties.
She'd still face **robots by 2039**, but values real skills.
**Children** feel possible again in this picture.

steps.text: Keep her furniture company job through the next few years
Learn joinery from her uncle Rafa on weekends
Plan with Mateo to start a family in two or three years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I don't want a handout from anyone, I want a job, and if the computers take mine I'll find work through my own family first. What would help is apprenticeships for adults and help for small family firms to take people on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about faith. Mine helps me not panic, even when I'm worried.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout from anyone, I want a job, and if the computers take mine I'll find work through my own family first.
portrait: Nora is a **27-year-old copywriter** at a family-owned furniture company, engaged to Mateo, an electrician.
She has **never used AI** and prefers writing about craft by hand.
She leans on **family and faith**, and wants work rather than handouts.
She is calm in the plateau but **alarmed** when AGI comes within five years.
Her fallback is **Mateo's business** and, with time, joinery with her uncle.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most because she'd **lose her job** before her new marriage is settled.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **adult apprenticeships** and support for small **family firms** to hire.
